Lorsqu’on entre dans le bâtiment de Peti: Walking into the Petites-Mains building, right across from Jarry Park, you immediately feel a wave of warmth and comfort wash over you. That's no accident: here, everyone, from the front-desk staff to the employees of the café-caterer, seems kind and cordial.
Petites-Mains, une entreprise d’insertio: Petites-Mains, a non-profit work-integration enterprise, was born out of a specific request: to help immigrant women integrate and gain independence. Permanent residents, refugees, asylum seekers and even women without status: women from immigrant backgrounds come through this organization and leave with their heads held high. La Converse met Abir Mansour Ali, a program participant who became a Petites-Mains employee, and Mariam Abdali, the organization's deputy director, who walked us through the mission she has supported for years.
Abir Mansour Ali est arrivée au Québec i: Abir Mansour Ali arrived in Quebec almost three years ago. “Two years and seven months,” she specifies with a laugh. She is in charge of hot meals for the Petites-Mains cafeteria and catering service.
Vêtue d’un tablier blanc agencé avec le: Dressed in a white apron that matches the beige scarf on her head, she welcomes us warmly to her workplace, the organization's café-caterer. “I was born in Djibouti and spent my whole life there, but I'm of Yemeni origin,” the 42-year-old mother confides. After applying to immigrate to several countries, Abir, her husband and their three children settled in Montréal, since she and her family speak only Arabic and French.
« Quand je suis arrivée ici, ça faisait: “When I got here, I hadn't done anything other than take care of my family for 17 years,” Abir begins. “The first three months in Montréal, I was terribly bored. I had nothing to do, and I didn't think I'd be able to find work because I had no experience, no diploma,” she recalls. Yet a new life in Canada was a chance for her to work and to help her family, caught in the conflict in Yemen, where <l1>one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, according to the UN</l1>, is raging.
Un jour, elle décide de se lancer. Elle: One day, she decides to take the leap. She leaves her home, gets on the bus in Saint-Laurent, the borough where she lives, and goes to various employment-assistance organizations for newcomers. By dint of showing up, attending training workshops and even taking classes to improve her English, Abir meets M<sup>s</sup>. Naïm of CARI Saint-Laurent. Naïm directs her to Petites-Mains when she learns that Abir loves to cook and has been doing it for her family for 17 years.
« Lorsque je suis arrivée chez Petites-M: “When I arrived at Petites-Mains, I had no experience. But everyone helped me. The managers and the trainers were very patient, and the other participants and I ended up becoming a family,” she remembers with a smile. After a few months, once Abir's paid training was over, the enterprise officially hired her as the person in charge of hot meals at the café-restaurant.
« Quand je suis venue ici avec mon mari,: “When I came here with my husband, I didn't know anyone. I had no friends and no family, apart from my children. Here, I met people who became more than colleagues: real friends!” she says, moved.
Plus tard, Abir aimerait ouvrir son prop: Someday, Abir would like to open her own Yemeni restaurant. “I want to buy a house for my family and work hard to open my restaurant one day,” she says, her eyes full of stars. “I'm happy. I'm living my dream life here, and it's thanks to the people I met at Petites-Mains. Here, I found my perfect fit,” she finishes in a joyful tone.
Des parcours comme celui d’Abir, il y en: Journeys like Abir's are plentiful at Petites-Mains. The genesis of this family goes back 20 years and was no accident.
En 1994, à la suite de la fermeture d’un: In 1994, after a food bank in the Côte-des-Neiges neighbourhood closed for lack of funding, the people who ran it noticed that the majority of their beneficiaries were immigrant women. “The first thing the founders asked themselves was: why? Why are they the ones who make up the majority of food bank users?” says M<sup>s</sup>. Abdali.
À la suite de ce questionnement, des ren: Following that question, meetings were held with these women to understand their needs. All of them, whether they were mothers, former entrepreneurs, seniors or young adults, were clear: the first need is to become more independent. The second is to integrate. To better meet these needs, Petites-Mains was born, seeking to offer these women concrete solutions to help them find their footing in a new environment, in a new country.
L’entreprise est située dans l’arrondiss: The enterprise is located in the Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension borough. (Photo: Amélie Rock, La Converse)
Sœur Denise Arsenault et Nahid Aboumanso: Sister Denise Arsenault and Nahid Aboumansour, the organization's founders, set up sewing machines in a small space in the Côte-des-Neiges borough. Sewing classes were offered free of charge to the women concerned to give them adequate training in the field. That is how Petites-Mains was born.
« Ici, on est comme une grande famille »: “Here, we're like one big family,” Mariam tells us passionately. “We ask women what they know how to do and what they like to do, and we try to combine that with their way of life in Quebec, in Montréal,” she sums up.
« À chaque fois qu’une femme entre dans: “Every time a woman walks into our building, she must leave with solutions”: that is the mission of the organization Mariam co-manages. “The best way to give solutions to newly arrived women is to give them tools. Something that can serve them in life outside, in the working world and in their personal lives,” she adds.
« Pour les nouveaux arrivants, la premiè: “For newcomers, the first barrier is often language,” Mariam points out. She herself arrived in Montréal at the age of nine after spending several years travelling between Lebanon and Iran, her two countries of origin. “We offer francization courses from the ministère de l'Immigration to make it easier for newly arrived women to integrate,” she continues. “Then, depending on each woman's needs, we adjust to give everyone the right training and the right employment-integration program,” she explains.
« Il y a des femmes qui viennent ici san: “There are women who come here with no experience at all, and others who arrive with plenty of diplomas that aren't recognized, but no Quebec experience. Our goal is to let all these women find the right fit by uncovering transferable skills, no matter their background,” Mariam affirms. For example, a woman who has managed her family's personal finances her whole life without ever having worked in the field has a skill considered transferable. “By offering this woman broader training in finance, we give her an alternative to her background deemed ‘irrelevant,’” she illustrates.
Petites-Mains offre aussi de l’aide aux: Petites-Mains also helps asylum seekers and people without status with the process of obtaining an open work or study permit, so they can become more financially independent while they wait for a decision on their situation.
Des nouvelles arrivantes en classe de fr: Newly arrived women in a francization class. (Photo: Amélie Rock, La Converse)
L’organisme offre des formations dans de: The organization offers training in specific fields, such as sewing and food service. Employment assistance programs are also available, and all participants are paid for their learning.
Un centre de la petite enfance (CPE) se: A early childhood centre (CPE) is also on site. Social and intercultural workers also work for Petites-Mains and offer support and follow-up to participants.
L’organisme dispose aussi d’un café-trai: The organization also has a café-caterer on the ground floor, where about ten women work in the kitchen and in customer service. “The catering service allows us to hire about ten people to meet our clients' needs,” the deputy director says.
Mariam Abdali, directrice adjointe de Pe: Mariam Abdali, deputy director of Petites-Mains. (Photo: Amélie Rock, La Converse)
Conscient que l’intégration est une rela: Aware that integration is a two-way relationship between the host society and the immigrant, the organization encourages participants to get involved in their own way, asking them in particular to share their knowledge, for example by preparing dishes, in the case of those who work in the kitchen.
« Petites-Mains a des ententes avec plus: “Petites-Mains has agreements with several businesses in different fields that are among our employer partners. That allows us to guarantee many participants a job once their training here is finished,” Mariam explains. For the organization, it's also a way of showing recognition to the women who come through the work-integration enterprise.
« En plus de formations dans des domaine: “On top of training in particular fields, we offer job-search training. We help women get a first Quebec work experience by helping them put together a résumé, prepare for an interview or approach potential employers,” the manager lists.
Celles pour qui ces expériences ne march: Those for whom these experiences don't necessarily work out in the long run, or who run into obstacles on the road to professional integration, can always come back to Petites-Mains. “When you enter the Petites-Mains family, you're in it for good,” Mariam assures us. “There are women who come back to see us years after we first met, and that's normal. Integration is never easy. There can be harder times,” she explains. She says the organization will always be there for those who have been part of it in the past.
- Environ 30 000 femmes ont bénéficié de: - About 30,000 women have benefited from the organization's services since it was created in 1995.
- Chaque année, 80 % des femmes qui suiv: - Every year, 80% of the women who take training through the Petites-Mains program find lasting employment immediately afterward.
